content: The selection and availability of implants and equipment for external and internal fixation vary significantly between countries and even among hospitals within the same country. The choice of implants is primarily influenced by the training and expertise of the surgeons, as well as the availability of resources. While no exhaustive list of hardware for fracture fixation is provided, it is expected that each country standardizes its requirements for implants and equipment sets based on local professional expertise. In many countries, low-cost metal implants are used with varying degrees of success. Over time, countries may address the quality assurance of these implants through appropriate mechanisms. Recognizing the presence or risk of spinal injury is critical across all levels of healthcare, and the only resource required for this is adequate training. Regular monitoring of neurological function, particularly during the acute phase of injury, is essential. Patients with acute cervical spinal cord injuries are at risk of severe hypotension and respiratory complications, which necessitate careful trauma management to prevent further neurological deterioration. The management of extremity injuries requires resources such as basic immobilization tools (e.g., slings, splints), spine boards, and techniques for hemorrhage control in pelvic fractures. Advanced interventions, such as external and internal fixation, tendon repair, and fasciotomy for compartment syndrome, are necessary at higher levels of care. Proper handling of immobilized patients to prevent complications, such as airway obstruction and inadequate ventilation, is critical. Diagnostic tools like plain X-rays remain widely used, while CT and MRI provide significant utility but are often cost-prohibitive. When deemed essential, these imaging modalities must be available on an emergency basis, functioning 24/7. The management of burns and wounds requires capabilities to assess burn depth and extent, which is essential at all healthcare levels. Basic clean or sterile dressing materials are necessary, with sterile dressings being preferred at higher levels of care. Debridement of necrotic tissue and escharotomy are essential at specialist and tertiary care hospitals, as is skin grafting for non-healing burn wounds. Early excision and grafting of full-thickness burns can reduce mortality and improve functional outcomes but require adequate safeguards for blood loss and resuscitation. Preventing burn wound contractures through splinting and physiotherapy is essential at all hospital levels, with reconstructive surgery being desirable at specialist hospitals and essential at tertiary care centers. Rehabilitation services are critical for maximizing recovery after acute treatment. Basic physiotherapy and occupational therapy for extremity injuries, including splinting and range-of-motion exercises, are essential at all hospital levels. While fully trained physiotherapists and occupational therapists are ideal, training key personnel in these skills can provide effective care. Prosthetic services, including fitting and maintenance, are essential at tertiary care facilities and desirable at specialist hospitals. Psychological counseling is also essential at all levels to address post-injury mental health challenges and assist patients in adjusting to disabilities. Specialized services, such as neuropsychology and speech pathology, are desirable at higher levels of care. Pain control and access to essential medicines are critical components of trauma care. The WHO Model List of Essential Medicines includes most drugs needed for trauma care, but availability remains limited, particularly in rural areas of low-income countries. These guidelines emphasize the importance of ensuring the availability of trauma-related essential medicines at appropriate levels of the healthcare system.
